items.weakness_text: A core issue with the evaluation framework is that a LLM is used to infer the class. There’s no guarantee that this LLM is good in inferring the correct class from the annotations.
items.ac_evidence: Furthermore, the concern regarding circularity in the sufficiency definition was acknowledged by the authors but only promised as a future revision, leaving the current theoretical foundation of the framework shaky.

items.weakness_text: The claim that “strong performance in downstream tasks may not correlate with adequate conceptual supervision” (l. 462/463) is too strong. Also, I’d like to note that these models often weigh the concepts or only use a subset of them on a per-instance basis. Thus, the conclusion seems not warranted. It’d be more meaningful to take, say, the top-5 concepts per image and try to see if models can infer the correct class.
The finding that (multimodal) LLMs work not that well to capture fine-grained details is well-known. The paper doesn’t provide a novel insight regarding this point.
The paper’s writing could overall be improved for clarity.
The definition of sufficiency is somewhat circular and lacks grounding in formal interpretability theory. It might mistake a good result for true understanding.
items.ac_evidence: Furthermore, the concern regarding circularity in the sufficiency definition was acknowledged by the authors but only promised as a future revision, leaving the current theoretical foundation of the framework shaky.

items.weakness_text: The five-stage annotation process (Background, Superclass, Salient, Detailed, Auxiliary) may heavily influence results. The robustness of findings to prompt variations or alternative hierarchies is unexplored.
items.ac_evidence: They also provided a justification for their five-stage refinement process, grounding it in existing methodologies.

items.weakness_text: Although the paper critiques “utility-as-proxy,” its proposed CRI metric is still accuracy-based, measuring recoverability of class labels rather than interpretive richness or human-understandable sufficiency.
items.ac_evidence: The authors successfully clarified the distinction between the CRI metric and the common "utility-as-proxy" assumption, explaining that CRI relies solely on textual concepts rather than supplementary visual imagery.

items.weakness_text: The current research strictly limits its focus to image data. Therefore, its effectiveness is uncertain for other forms, such as text, tabular data, time series, or mixed-media reasoning.

The paper initially discusses annotations for both LLMs and VLMs; however, the proposed methodology and experiments focus only on the explanation of vision tasks with VLMs, without evaluating textual explanation tasks or reporting results for LLMs.

The reliability of the concept-chain gathering process and the CRI metric as accurate measures of “semantic sufficiency” remains unclear, as they have not been rigorously validated through human evaluation.
items.ac_evidence: The most critical concern—the lack of human validation—remains outstanding.
